Thank you. In that case, I would like to invite Mr. Kaushik Basu to provide the observations and intervention and also answer the questions made by delegations. Thank you.

Thank you very much. This was actually a very, very heartening meeting and interaction, and the positive comments made one feel that there is a need, palpable around the world, people are feeling for newer measures. The questions, I don't want to get into the details because broadly what the questions are addressing are matters that we are taking into account. For instance, people do point out and ask, is this going to be country ownership or international? The ownership will be at the level of the nation, but there is an international aspect as well, which is extremely important, and I think international organizations will have to be involved. What we did not go into here, but Nora will recall, we've had lots of discussions, that many of the measures that one country takes has externalities and spillovers for other countries. There, automatically, there is an international dimension to it, which will have to come in. And we are hoping that we touch on this and that will be picked up. And therefore, This is not something just for professional economists. This is for nations, national policymakers and leaders, for international policymakers and statisticians around the world. There was one very pointed question apart from this, which came from Mexico, and I'll just give a short answer to that and I'll stop. Where Mexico asked, have we identified political challenges? To that, the response is right now, no, because this broad aspiration of what we are trying as part of the HLEG is in keeping with what nations are trying. But I do anticipate that there will be political challenges once the measures are out there. And some countries on some dimensions will some years do well, some years do poorly. And it is a very natural tendency that when you do poorly on some measure, you resist the measure itself. So the political challenges will come, which is just as well. It suggests that we are doing something important, which even if politically for a moment we resist, we should have a broader, larger sense to realize that we are aspiring towards something which is useful for the world, useful for the planet. Thank you.
I thank you, Excellency. I now invite Ms. Nora Lustig to provide observations and also may answer some of the questions on intervention made by delegations.

Thank you very much. I want to echo Kaushik's comment about how heartening this meeting has been, the fact that it's so well attended, so many people wanted to express their opinion. It's impossible, as you can imagine, to address all the questions within the time frame that we have, but we take them very seriously. And I just want to highlight a couple of things. One is that the format of the release of the report will be announced shortly. through the Secretariat and the UN channels, and there will be time allocated for a process in which Member States can look at the report and prepare their remarks. But we don't have a fixed timeline yet, but it will be shortly communicated. The other thing I wanted to say about country ownership, that's absolutely essential, we are consistently emphasizing the fact that the indicators have to be country owned. And also what we're proposing should not be seen, like I said, as the end of a process and also as the end of the indicators that countries will be monitoring. We want to provide something that could be a core set of indicators and then, depending on the country, there may be additional ones different ones that want to be used to continue monitoring progress in the specific circumstances of that country. I also want to add something about a role of the multi, the international bodies here. I think it would be great as it's been done with GDP and many indicators that are in the SDGs to have norms, conventions, protocols, and how things should be measured so we can compare. And that's a very important role that the UN has been playing through its statistical commission that would continue to have a very active role to ensure that what we're proposing that is new also falls into that kind of process so that there are guidelines And there are ways in which in the end we can compare the results. Regarding the specific existing multidimensional indices, we are looking at them. We've been in particular having lots of conversations with the Human Development Report Office that have been very interesting to see to what extent down the road we can converge to a common indicator That would be part of the family and also include incorporate many of the new things that have been developing in the literature on how to measure multi dimensional well, being. There, about political challenges, we did not incorporate that in our mandate. Well, it was not in our mandate, and I don't think we are the best people to assess that. I think it's something that will happen in the process of, hopefully, widespread uptake of what we're proposing. And also, I want to emphasize again that we're proposing outcome indicators, so Some of the interventions mentioned what we call enablers, like the importance of technological change and the quality of the state institutions, et cetera. Those are fundamental, but at least in my view, they need a different parallel process in identifying what are the drivers of the outcomes and how we're going to monitor whether those drivers are happening or not, and let me stop here. And thanks again.
I think, Nora. I think we have completed, and I would like to now invite Ms. Amina Mohamed, Deputy Secretary General, to provide her observations and also to deliver some closing remarks.

Thank you very much, Mr. President, and thank you to our co-facilitators, but mostly thank you for all of those that have attended and the meaningful contributions that we have heard this afternoon. There are many challenges facing us, and often when I am speaking with Member States, you asked. We should not forget that we have outcomes from last year's major conferences that we also have to follow up on, and we have so much more to do to reach the 2030 agenda. Last year, what was meaningful in terms of the work that we have done, and it aligns with what we are trying to do on beyond GDP that came out of the pact, is the FFD4 in Seville and the platform for action, but also Doha, where it was important the inequalities discussion and the jobs, and Belem on the environment and climate. So important work that continues to be done by us all. And this meeting today, I think, pulls a very important thread of how we measure these commitments when we do implement them. And I hope that we will be able to engage you further as the report is released and the intergovernmental process starts. And this both in New York, but also in our other in our other places of work in Geneva, in Vienna, at the country level, across the world. I would, you know, again, just re-underscoring what my colleagues, participants have said, really important, the national ownership. And so therefore, we will put at the disposal of member states that connection through the RSCs and the UN country teams to continue this discussion guided by the report and the work of our experts. There has been a call, continuously, today and before, for support to the statistical commissions. This is not to overburden them. Of course, it will be more work, because we are trying to broaden those measures to be relevant in the lives of people and in the environment that we live in. However, I think that we will do so much more to lift what is needed for systems, not just the capacities of individuals but also the systems that need to to make this work. We are aligning with the many other measures that were mentioned by our member states today, including the MDVI, our multidimensional vulnerability index, the gender, and others. And we are absolutely sure that we are not replacing GDP. We are, in fact, reinforcing, strengthening that measure. Out of Seville came the Global Alliance, and we look forward to working closely with you so that we are ensured that the network that has come behind this helps us to reinforce the voice on the floor. As was indicated by many Member States, not everyone has the capacities available to them to engage, so the more we find the support for this, the better. There was a question from Panama about some additional, quite a bit of additional information that will come in due course, and I hope very quickly as we launch the report. But in the meantime, just to direct all of you to our website, it is really comprehensive. Everything is loaded up there. But I was also wondering, perhaps we could offer an updated fact sheet so that that helps to fill some of the gaps before, of course, the report comes out. But with that, I encourage everyone to engage with us, to engage with the intergovernmental process, of course, and messaging to our countries' capitals that this work now is coming to a space where we can now give input for discussions to happen. And I think as Professor Lustig said to us, it's the beginning. of another part of this discussions that have gone on for many years, but perhaps now we can begin to see how we implement. I think the dashboard, the additional minimal indicators that we talk about, begins for the rubber to hit the road beyond the research and the processes and the discussions. I think now is the time when we will need to make some move forward in this work that has been on the road for a long time. So our full support to everyone, and we very much look forward to continuing this discussion. And thank you for the space to hear you and to help inform the report as it comes out in the next few weeks. Thank you.

I thank the Deputy Secretary General. With this, I would like to express my appreciation to the Deputy Secretary General the Co-Chairs and the High-Level Expert Group, the Under-Secretary-General of DESA, and to all participants for their contribution to this meeting. The informal meeting of the plenary is now concluded. The meeting is adjourned.
